summary: Describes general considerations for deploying a stateful Path Computation Element, which tracks path state to do traffic-engineering calculations. It covers benefits, challenges and limitations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A planner who remembers every route in use can plan better trips. This explains when having such a planner helps and what difficulties come with it.

questions: what is an lsp state database
subtitle: Why a path computation server that remembers every active tunnel can plan a network better, and what it costs.

tldr.problem: A stateless Path Computation Element (PCE) answers each request without knowing about the other Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in the network, so requests arrive in random order and the result can be wasteful or unpredictable.
tldr.mechanism: A stateful PCE keeps an LSP State Database next to its Traffic Engineering Database, so it can compute paths with all active LSPs in view. An active stateful PCE can also take control of LSPs delegated to it.
tldr.outcome: The RFC walks through use cases such as throughput, recovery, reoptimization and defragmentation, and notes the costs: state synchronization, a PCE view that lags the network, and extra attack surface.

facts.label: Delegation
facts.value: An LSP is delegated to only one PCE at a time

today: RFC 8051 is an Informational document published in January 2017, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines no protocol itself; the PCEP extensions for stateful PCE are covered in separate documents.

sections.title: Why Remember Path State
sections.content:
The PCE architecture in RFC 4655 lets a Path Computation Element (PCE) compute Traffic Engineering paths (MPLS and GMPLS TE LSPs). A PCE keeps the network topology and resource information in its TE Database (TED). RFC 5440 defines PCEP, the protocol a Path Computation Client (PCC) uses to talk to a PCE.

A PCE can be stateless or stateful. A stateful PCE adds a second store, the LSP State Database (LSP-DB), holding attributes of all active LSPs: their paths, bandwidth use, switching types and constraints. That lets it consider individual LSPs and how they depend on each other.

The price is reliable state synchronization between the PCE and the network, between PCE and PCCs, and between cooperating PCEs, with control-plane overhead and a large amount of state to keep. This document covers benefits and limits through use cases. Stateless alternatives are mentioned where they exist. The PCEP extensions are covered elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: A planner with a notebook of every route in use can avoid clashes. Keeping the notebook up to date is extra work, though.

sections.title: Passive, Active and Delegated
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms that the use cases depend on.

  • Stateful PCE: has access to the network state and to the set of active paths and their reserved resources. It may also retain information about LSPs under construction to reduce churn and resource contention.
  • Passive Stateful PCE: uses LSP state learned from PCCs to optimize path computations, but does not actively update LSP state.
  • Active Stateful PCE: may issue recommendations to the network, for example by using delegation to update LSP parameters in PCCs that hand control of their LSPs to it.
  • Delegation: granting a PCE temporary rights to modify a subset of LSP parameters. The PCC that owns the LSP state has the right to delegate it, and an LSP is owned by a single PCC at any time. For intra-domain LSPs this PCC should be the head end.
  • PCE Initiation: assuming delegation is granted by default, a PCE can issue recommendations to the network.
sections.plainLanguage: A passive planner only takes notes and gives advice when asked. An active planner can also move the pieces, but only on routes the owner has handed over.

sections.title: Better LSP Placement
sections.content:
The first group of use cases argues for visibility into global LSP state and for PCE control over the order and timing of LSP changes. In RFC 5440, LSP changes are driven by PCReq messages under a PCC's local timers, so reservations arrive in randomized order. The main benefit comes from moving away from this asynchronous PCC-driven mode toward central control, focused on the active stateful model.

  • Throughput and bin packing: in the RFC's example topology, a stateless PCE leaves throughput at 50% of optimal. Throughput maximization often becomes a bin-packing problem, which is NP-hard, but common heuristics run in polynomial time.
  • Deadlock: RSVP-TE implementations generally do not tear down an established LSP when a bandwidth increase fails, so an out-of-profile LSP can hurt in-profile LSPs and make the TED inaccurate. Global LSP visibility plus placing LSPs on disjoint links would isolate the damage.
  • Minimum perturbation: a low-priority LSP can be set up and then preempted by a more important one moments later. A stateful PCE computes both together and can find the minimum number of lower priority LSPs to reroute with make-before-break.
  • Predictability: the same two LSPs can end up on very different paths depending on which is signaled first, which makes simulation hard. An active stateful PCE can order computations and setup deterministically.
sections.plainLanguage: If cars enter a parking lot in random order, spaces get wasted. A parking attendant who sees the whole lot can fit more cars and move fewer of them.

sections.title: More Use Cases: Sizing, Recovery and Cleanup
sections.content:
The remaining scenarios show where state helps beyond placement.

  • Auto-bandwidth adjustment: the head end normally watches usage and asks for a recomputation. With an active stateful PCE, resizing can be decided by an external entity that knows historical trends, application demands and policy.
  • Bandwidth scheduling: a passive stateful PCE can keep scheduled LSPs and their resource use, which needs coarse time synchronization between PCEs and PCCs. With PCE initiation it can trigger setup and deletion without changing head-end behavior.
  • Recovery: for protection, the LSP-DB lets the PCE avoid giving shared backup resources to LSPs that might fail together. For restoration after a link failure, PCCs can send LSP identifiers instead of full details and the PCE can recompute affected LSPs concurrently. For SRLG diversity, the PCC can name already established LSPs by identifier only.
  • Virtual Network Topology maintenance, LSP reoptimization (including the Global Concurrent Optimization of RFC 5557), and resource defragmentation, including optical spectrum in flexible-grid networks.
  • Point-to-multipoint: messages can refer to an LSP by identifier and carry only changes to the tree.
  • Impairment-aware routing and wavelength assignment in optical networks: the PCE can use stored LSP impairment information rather than extending routing protocols to flood it.
sections.plainLanguage: Knowing what is already booked also helps with backup plans, reshuffling, and tidying up gaps so big requests still fit.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
Stateless and stateful PCEs can coexist, and multiple stateful PCEs can too, for redundancy, load sharing or splitting computation features. Discovery or configuration can tell the two types apart. An LSP is delegated to only one PCE at a time, though it can be redelegated, for example when a PCE fails. RFC 7399 discusses synchronizing state among PCEs.

The LSP-DB is populated from PCC information, so the PCE view lags behind the true network state. A stateful PCE therefore reduces but cannot eliminate crankbacks, and cannot guarantee optimal results every time. When PCEs with different capabilities cooperate, referring to an LSP by a unique identifier is useful.

After a restart, a PCE must resynchronize LSP state. It can reacquire it from network nodes or other PCEs, restore it from a local backup, or use a hybrid. Local recovery still needs some resynchronization, and resynchronization may add load and delay.
sections.plainLanguage: The planner's notebook is always a little behind real life, and if the planner is away, someone has to refill the notebook before work continues.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document defines no new PCEP extensions. It notes that the PCEP extensions for a stateful PCE and for delegation of path control give a hypothetical adversary more information and control, and create additional attack surfaces. That includes authentication and encryption of PCEP sessions and snooping on the state of active LSPs. Documents that define the PCEP extensions need to consider these risks.
sections.plainLanguage: A planner who knows and controls everything is a juicy target, so the line to the planner must be locked down.
